title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–20)
hook: now read the parable with the explanation beside it
tomorrow: the seed that grows while you sleep

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is my mother: a family widened to everyone who does God's will. Your line was family by doing God's will. Which stranger did you treat as kin? Day two hundred one.

You've heard this story before on the path. Back in the stories camp, we met the sower in Matthew's gospel: a farmer flinging seed, some on the path, some on rock, some in thorns, some on good soil. That time, we heard it as a story. Today we're reading Mark straight through, so we meet it again, in Mark's own words, and this time we're going to do what a good reader does: lay the story side by side with the explanation Jesus gives his friends afterward, and look closely at one kind of ground. Today: the sower again.
screen: `WE'VE MET HIM BEFORE.` → `NOW IN MARK'S WORDS.` → `STORY AND EXPLANATION, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The crowd is so big that Jesus gets into a boat and sits on the water, teaching the people on the shore. Then he begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hear ye: Behold, the sower went out to sow." Four kinds of ground. Seed on the path is eaten by birds. Seed on rock springs up fast and withers in the sun, with no root. Seed among thorns is choked. Seed on good ground yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. And he ends: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Second, the explanation. Later, alone with the twelve, Jesus explains it line by line. The seed is the word. The path is the person the word never gets into. The rock is the one who welcomes it with joy but falls away when trouble comes. And good ground is the one who hears, receives, and bears fruit. Third, the thorns. Look at these closely, because they're the ones most of us live among. "And the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts after other things entering in choke the word, and it is made fruitless." Notice: the thorns don't kill the seed on the first day. The seed sprouts. It grows. It's just slowly crowded out by worry, by money, by wanting other things, until nothing comes of it. Nobody decides to stop listening. It gets choked. Fourth, the harvest. A hundredfold would likely have sounded astonishing to people who farmed that land. The parable ends not in failure but in more than anyone expected.
screen: `A BOAT FOR A PULPIT.` · `PATH, ROCK, THORNS, GOOD GROUND.` · `THE THORNS: WORRY, MONEY, WANTING.` · `A HARVEST NOBODY EXPECTED.` · then, large: `THE CARES OF THE WORLD CHOKE THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the thorns in your week. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days. What choked the good things? Not a disaster, just the slow crowding. A worry you kept circling. Money on your mind. Wanting something so much it filled the room. Name one thorn. Don't pull it out yet. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can show it to God. If you don't, just notice how much room it takes up. The bell holds the time.
The sower again. The parable of four kinds of ground, read now in Mark, with Jesus's own explanation beside it. Today's word.
Your line: the thorns are the cares. Today, when one worry starts crowding everything else, name it as a thorn, and give the good seed a little room. Day two hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and many use it for lectio divina, asking which kind of ground they are right now.

fork.setup: you're the seed, and you've sprouted among thorns. nobody has stepped on you and the sun hasn't burned you. what happens?
options: you grow into a great harvest.
the thorns grow up and slowly choke you.

original.note: Greek: thorns, the thistles and briars that choke the growing seed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a farming story about seeds.
what it means: the same word lands differently; the thorns are the everyday cares that slowly choke it.
what a scholar hears: one of the few parables the gospels explain allegorically; a hundredfold is an extraordinary yield.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 4:3 and 4:19 given from memory; confirm.
The hook refers back to the Matthew version of the sower in camp 2 (the outline's 'The sower (Matthew 13:1–23)'); confirm the day is taught before this one on the Catholic path.
Hundredfold as 'astonishing': ancient yield estimates vary (often cited as around tenfold for good years); stated loosely.
Mark 4:10–12 (the purpose of parables, quoting Isaiah) is not discussed.
